newsitem.title: CHINA: China in spring "Strike Hard" crime crackdown.
newsitem.headline: China in spring "Strike Hard" crime crackdown.

text.p: China has launched a spring season "Strike Hard" crackdown on crime to battle an evil that last week drew the ire of 40 percent of the usually rubber-stamp parliament and is among the top grievances of average Chinese.
With the completion of the December-February winter phase of the Strike Hard crackdown, the Ministry of Public Security had now launched its spring assault, the Xinhua news agency said on Monday.
The main thrust of the spring crackdown would be bomb attacks and bank robberies, the ministry revealed.
Bomb attacks have been rare in China, but two bombings in the last month have grabbed attention, particularly among Beijing residents who have long considered their city one of the world's safest.
Police in the capital have been on high alert since an explosion from a homemade bomb ripped through a public bus in one of Beijing's busiest commercial districts two weeks ago.
Sources said at least two people were killed by the bomb.

That explosion followed a carefully organised attack in the far western, restive Xinjiang region, when three bombs exploded on three buses, killing nine and injuring 74 on the day China was holding final funeral rites for late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Mafia-style gangs would be another major target of the spring crackdown, due to run until May, along with prostitution, gambling and drugs, Xinhua said.
Police would also focus their search for illegal guns, ammunition and explosives in regions where social order was in particular chaos, the report said but did not elaborate.
Security authorities reported successes in the winter phase of the crackdown launched last April 1, but said a tough task lay ahead for spring.
"It is not easy to be optimistic about the current situation of social order," Xinhua quoted a police official as saying.
The Ministry of Public Security reported police had cracked 380,000 crimes from December to the end of February, including 145,000 major crimes.
Police had uncovered 51,000 gangs, including 133 mafia-style underworld gangs, Xinhua said.
In the first three months of the Strike Hard crackdown last year, police reported 162,000 arrests. Thousands are believed to have been executed since China decided to get tough on crime.
China launched Strike Hard to try to curb a rising tide of crime and restore confidence in the ruling party.

That drop in confidence was reflected in a vote in the usually docile National People's Congress, or parliament, on Friday when only 59.6 percent of deputies supported a report on achievements to eradicate crime by the top prosecutor.
Nearly one-third showed their dissatisfaction with the report by the top judge but deputies overwhelmingly passed a new, tougher crime law expected to increase the number of capital crimes.
The changes drag the 17-year-old criminal code into the 1990s by listing offences such as money laundering, computer crime and insider trading.
Public opinion polls show rising crime is the chief grievance of many Chinese.
Beijing leaders have made clear that reinforcing social stability and cracking down on graft will both be priorities in the period following Deng's death on February 19.
